concept.name: Commodity trading advisor
concept.definition: A commodity trading advisor (CTA) is a person who, for compensation or profit, directly or indirectly advises others as to the value of or the advisability of trading futures contracts, commodity options, or swaps, or issues analyses or reports concerning them; advising indirectly includes exercising trading authority over a customer's account. CTAs generally must register with the CFTC (CEA Section 1a(12)) and become NFA members.
concept.intuition: A CTA is a professional futures-market advisor or manager: clients pay them to recommend or run futures trading strategies, similar to how an investment adviser handles securities.
concept.mechanics: CTAs either publish advice or manage client accounts under power of attorney (managed accounts), charging management and often performance fees. Registration requires proficiency testing, disclosure documents describing strategy, risks, fees, and performance, and ongoing CFTC/NFA compliance; many hedge fund managers are registered as CTAs or CPOs.
concept.failure_modes: CTA performance is strategy-dependent and often trend-following, producing long flat or losing stretches in range-bound markets; disclosed past performance is not predictive. Fraud or inadequate disclosure remains a risk, mitigated by NFA oversight but not eliminated.
concept.misconceptions: 'CTA' is a regulatory registration category, not proof of a profitable strategy or a quality mark. Also, CTAs need not advise on commodities only — the category covers advice on financial futures, FX, and swaps as well.
concept.example: A registered CTA manages a $50 million managed-futures program, trading diversified futures trends across energy, rates, and currencies, and charges clients a 2% management fee plus 20% of new profits.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
